one_liner: 2016 AVX512F SWAR versions of strlen, strchr, strrchr and strcmp; 4-16x over a 2016 glibc on Knights Landing.
what_it_does: Four standalone C++ functions (avx512f_strlen, avx512f_strchr, avx512f_strrchr, avx512f_strcmp), each a small .cpp file that the test and speed programs #include directly; there is no header or library. They mimic the libc signatures except that strchr/strrchr take a char instead of an int and return char*. They are research toys from Wojciech Mula's snippet repository, written for Xeon Phi Knights Landing, whose AVX-512F has no byte-granularity compares.
how_it_is_fast: Each loop iteration loads 64 bytes with an unaligned _mm512_loadu_si512 and applies the classic SWAR zero-byte test ((v - 0x01010101) & ~v & 0x80808080, fused into one vpternlogd) to 16 dwords at once, giving a 16-bit dword mask; strchr/strrchr run the same test on v XOR a broadcast of the character, and strcmp combines s1's zero mask with a dword-inequality mask (vpcmpneqd). Once a mask bit fires, a short scalar check of the 4 bytes of that dword finds the exact position, and strrchr uses clz on the mask to find the last match per block. The loop body has no per-byte work, so long strings run at about 12-16 GB/s versus 0.7-3 GB/s for the libc baseline in the author's run.
when_to_use: As a reference or starting point for SWAR-in-SIMD string scanning on AVX-512F-only targets (Knights Landing/Knights Mill) where byte compares (AVX-512BW) are missing.
Long ASCII strings (kilobytes) held in buffers you control and pad with at least 64 readable bytes past the terminator, where a 4-16x scan speedup over an old SSE2-era libc matters.
Teaching material: each kernel is 30-100 lines and shows mask-based early exit, dword-to-byte refinement and the last-match trick for strrchr.
when_not_to_use: As a general libc replacement: the kernels read up to 63 bytes past the terminator (and past the first difference in strcmp) with no page-boundary handling, so a string ending near the end of a mapped page can fault.

Non-ASCII data or a NUL search character: strchr/strrchr miss matches for characters 0x80-0xFF, strchr(s, 0) and strrchr(s, 0) return NULL, and strcmp orders bytes 0x80-0xFF as negative (see gotchas).

CPUs with AVX-512BW/VL (Skylake-SP and later, Zen 4): byte compares make the SWAR detour unnecessary, and current glibc already selects EVEX string variants there; nothing here was measured on such hardware.
Short strings (tens of bytes), which dominate real strlen/strcmp calls: the benchmark measured only average lengths of about 5-10 KB, and per-call overhead and the scalar tail were not studied.
Projects needing maintenance or a build system: the code dates from October 2016, the README calls the tests 'not very good', and there is no packaging beyond a Makefile.

integration.min_toolchain: C++14 as the Makefile builds it (-std=c++14 -mavx512f -O3); GCC or Clang for __builtin_ctz/__builtin_clz and __attribute__((always_inline)); measured with GCC 5.4.3
integration.platforms: x86-64 with AVX-512F only (Knights Landing used for the numbers; Intel SDE suggested for emulation)
integration.thread_safety: stateless pure functions, safe to call concurrently
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — libc-like names and results only for ASCII strings, non-NUL search characters and buffers padded by 64 bytes; strchr/strrchr take char rather than int

gotchas: Correctness bug (found by exact emulation of the kernels' 32-bit lane arithmetic): avx512f_strchr and avx512f_strrchr build the broadcast pattern as 0x01010101u * uint32_t(c) with c a signed char, so a character >= 0x80 sign-extends (0xE9 becomes 0xE8E8E8E9). A match is then seen only in byte 0 of each dword: occurrences at byte offsets 1-3 are missed (NULL returned), and a byte equal to c-1 at offsets 1-3 trips assert(false), which aborts because the Makefile does not define NDEBUG. The benchmark searches only for 'X' (0x58), so the timing is unaffected.

avx512f_strchr(s, '\0') and avx512f_strrchr(s, '\0') return NULL instead of a pointer to the terminator, and avx512f_strcmp compares bytes as signed char (int a = c1[i]), so "caf\xC3\xA9" vs "cafe" returns -162 where libc strcmp returns a positive value. test.cpp misses all of this: it uses only '?', 'X' and 0, compares strcmp results for exact equality, and its strchr test only places 'X' after the terminator, so the found path is never validated.

Harness flaw in speed_strrchr.cpp: the loop writes 'X' at every index i and then restores '?', including i = size-1 where the only terminator sits, so after the first of the 5 iterations the 10 KiB buffer (plus its 64-byte '?' padding) has no NUL. Both std::strrchr and the AVX512F version then read past the heap allocation until they hit a stray zero byte (undefined behaviour). Both sides do it, so the ratio probably holds, but 4 of the 5 timed passes run on unterminated strings.

Every call in all four harnesses starts at the same buffer start (plain new char[], not forced to 64-byte alignment), lengths are uniform over 0-10 KiB (strrchr always scans the full 10 KiB), the 10 KiB buffer stays cache-resident, and timing is a single gettimeofday interval per implementation with no repetitions.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it only to study or adapt the AVX-512F SWAR technique (Knights Landing-class hardware); for a production x86 replacement use AOCL-LibMem or Agner Fog's asmlib, which dispatch by CPU and cover many more functions, and for Arm use Arm Optimized Routines.
verified_claims_summary: In the author's single October 2016 run on a Xeon Phi 7210 (Knights Landing) with GCC 5.4.3 and -O3 -mavx512f, 5 passes over a 10 KiB buffer took 0.0829 s with libc strlen vs 0.0167 s (4.96x), strchr 0.1000 vs 0.0225 s (4.44x), strrchr 0.7211 vs 0.0450 s (16.03x) and strcmp 0.1171 vs 0.0297 s (3.94x); about 0.7-3.2 GB/s for libc vs 9-16 GB/s for AVX512F (derived from the harness's byte counts). The glibc version and which variant it picked on KNL are not stated; a 2016 glibc probably ran an SSE2 path (inference).
status_note: Untouched since a 2020 strcmp simplification (core code from October 2016) in a BSD-2-Clause snippet repository; small enough to copy, but fix the signed-char broadcast, NUL-character and strcmp sign bugs and add page-safe tail handling before using it on real data.
